transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I’ve been getting stuck in these little routines. I wash my hands again after handling my wrist brace, and I keep rechecking the stove and the front door. Sometimes I silently count through steps before I leave the house. It’s not extreme, but it’s starting to make me late, even when I know I’ve already done enough.
Do you have unwanted or intrusive thoughts that come to mind that make you feel anxious or uncomfortable?

Yes. I’ll be reading at home, or getting ready to go in for a museum shift, and this unpleasant thought barges in that I’ve left something unsafe, or touched something dirty, or somehow put someone else at risk. I know it’s probably out of proportion, but it still makes me anxious.
Do these routines or thoughts take up a lot of your time, or do they cause you a lot of distress even if you try to resist them?

It does take time, yes. I’m still managing on my own, but it’s made me late to my docent shifts a few times. And I’ve skipped a few museum events because just getting out the door felt like too much with all the checking and routines. So it’s not taking over my life, but it is getting in the way.
Have you ever tried to stop or change these routines or thoughts, and if so, what happens when you try?

Yes, I have tried. I’ll tell myself, “You already checked the stove,” or “Your hands are clean enough,” and try to just leave it alone. But then I get this nagging feeling that I missed something, and I end up going back to check the front door or washing again after touching my wrist brace. If I don’t do the little counting steps before leaving, I feel unsettled, like I can’t quite trust that I’m ready to go. It’s not a huge production, but it does slow me down.
How much time do these routines and thoughts take up during the day — do you ever find that they add up to an hour or more?

I haven’t timed it carefully. It’s enough that I’m still managing at home, but it does add up when I’m trying to leave. I’ve been late to my docent shifts because of it, and I’ve skipped a few museum events when getting out the door just felt like too much. So, yes, it’s interfering, even if I’m not sure exactly how many minutes.
Are these intrusive thoughts and routines mostly about specific themes, like safety, contamination, or orderliness, or do they vary a lot in content?

They’re mostly in a few areas, I’d say. Safety is a big one — like I’ll be reading at home or getting ready to go to the museum, and this thought barges in that I left something unsafe. Then there’s the unclean feeling after I’ve touched something. And sometimes it’s this worry that I’ve somehow put someone else at risk, even though I know it’s out of proportion. It doesn’t feel random so much as those themes repeating.

Do the intrusive thoughts about safety, contamination, or responsibility come up first and lead you to perform the checking or washing routines, or do the routines come first without being connected to a specific thought?

Usually the thought comes first. I’ll get the feeling that maybe the stove or the front door isn’t really okay, or that my hands aren’t clean after handling my wrist brace, and then I go back and check or wash again.

With the counting before I leave, it’s a little more like a routine I feel I have to do so I can trust I’m ready. Even when I know I’ve already done enough, I still get stuck in it, and that’s what’s been making me late.
Do you ever find yourself dwelling on certain thoughts or ideas for long periods, trying to figure them out or make sense of them, even when you wish you could stop thinking about them?

Yes. I’ll be reading at home, or getting ready for a museum shift, and this ugly little thought keeps barging in — that I’ve left something unsafe, or touched something unclean, or somehow put someone at risk. I know, logically, it’s out of proportion, but I still end up turning it over in my mind longer than I want to.
Do you find yourself going over these thoughts again and again in your mind, trying to figure them out or reassure yourself, even when you wish you could stop thinking about them?

Yes, I do. It’s like I’ll be trying to read, or I’m getting ready for my museum shift, and the thought keeps coming back — maybe I left something unsafe, or touched something unclean, or somehow put someone at risk. I know it’s out of proportion, but I still go over it in my head trying to feel sure.
When these intrusive thoughts come up or you feel the urge to do one of these routines, do you feel increased anxiety or distress if you try to resist them or stop yourself from doing the routine?

Yes. If I try not to do it, I get pretty uncomfortable. It’s not always a huge panic, but it builds enough that I have trouble just leaving it alone.

I’ll think, “I already checked,” but then I’m stuck wanting to wash again, or look at the stove or the door again, or count through the steps before I leave. If I don’t, I keep feeling like something isn’t settled, and that’s when I end up being late.
On average, do these thoughts or routines take up more than an hour of your day?

Most days, yes, it probably adds up to more than an hour. It’s not one long stretch, but all the little routines pile up — washing my hands again after handling my wrist brace, rechecking the stove and the front door, counting through what I need to do before I leave. I know I’ve usually done enough, but I still get stuck, and it’s been making me late.
Do these intrusive thoughts and routines feel like they are connected to a bigger worry or fear that you can't quite control, or do they feel more like habits that you've developed over time?

I think it’s more tied to a worry I can’t quite shake than just a habit. I get stuck doing the routines — washing my hands again after touching my wrist brace, checking the stove and front door, counting through the steps before I leave — because I’m trying to feel sure everything is okay. Even when I know I’ve already done enough, it doesn’t feel settled, and then I end up running late.
Do the intrusive thoughts or routines take up more than an hour of your day most days?

Yes, most days it does. It’s all the little things adding up — washing my hands again after I handle my wrist brace, checking the stove and front door more than once, and counting through things before I leave. It starts to take enough time that I’m late, even though I know I’ve already done what I needed to do.
